posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the pin setter)
posts.quote: SETTING PINS AT THE BOWLING ALLEY PAID A DIME A LINE AND TAUGHT A BOY TO DUCK.
posts.caption: Before the machines took over, the pins at the bowling alley were set by hand, and the hands belonged to boys of about fourteen. You sat on a little ledge above the pit, and when the ball came thundering down the lane, you pulled your feet up and waited. Then you hopped down, gathered the pins, set them back on their spots, and rolled the ball back up the return. A good setter could do a whole line in under a minute. The league bowlers never saw our faces, only the pins popping up in the dark. We went home with sore arms, a few bruises, and a pocket full of dimes that felt like a fortune.
posts.first: I set pins two winters at the lanes on Main Street. I still flinch a little when I hear a strike. The owner kept a jar of root beer in the back for us, and that jar was worth more than the dimes.

posts.quote: WE CHECKED EVERY COIN RETURN WE PASSED, AND ABOUT ONCE A YEAR IT PAID OFF.
posts.caption: You never walked past a pay phone without sliding two fingers into the little silver slot at the bottom. Most days it was empty and a little sticky. But sometimes, just sometimes, there was a dime sitting there, left behind by a stranger in a hurry. That was a whole afternoon of candy money, found fair and square. We checked at the bus station, the drugstore, the gas station, and the phone outside the church. A kid with a good eye and a steady habit could clear nearly a dollar in a summer.
posts.first: My brother found a quarter once in the booth outside the lumberyard and talked about it for a month. He told it so many times that the coin grew a little each time. I still reach for those slots out of habit.

posts.quote: Somebody on every block kept a basement full of folding chairs, and they got borrowed for every wedding and funeral.
posts.first: Ours were stacked behind the furnace at my uncle's house, each one stenciled with the name of the church. They went out in the back of a pickup and came back with a casserole smell on them.

posts.quote: OUR TOWN GOT ITS FIRST TRAFFIC LIGHT IN 1962, AND HALF THE TOWN CAME OUT TO WATCH IT CHANGE.
posts.caption: The county put up the first traffic light at the corner of Main and Third on a Saturday morning, and by noon there was a crowd. Men stood on the curb with their hats pushed back and their arms folded. The barber came out with a towel still over his shoulder. When the light went from green to yellow to red, a little cheer went up, like a rocket had left the ground. Then somebody's pickup stopped and waited for it, and everybody agreed that this was the future. For a week, people drove around the block just to get stopped.
posts.first: My grandfather said it was a waste of good tax money and then drove through it four times that first day. I think he just wanted to see it work. We still call that corner the light.

posts.quote: THE PENCIL SHARPENER WAS BOLTED TO THE WALL, AND THE LONG WALK TO IT WAS THE BEST PART OF THE DAY.
posts.caption: Every classroom had one hand-crank sharpener bolted to the wall by the door, and it was the most visited spot in the room. Nobody's pencil was ever dull enough to need it, but a hundred pencils got a little shorter anyway. You raised your hand, got the nod, and walked the long way past every desk on the aisle. You gave the crank a slow turn and listened to the grinding all the way down to a perfect point. Then you took a good look out the window before you walked back. The shavings smelled like cedar, and the tray underneath was emptied by whichever kid the teacher trusted most.
posts.first: Our teacher kept a coffee can of stubby pencils by hers, and the sharpener was the one thing nobody was allowed to touch without permission. I wore mine down to the size of a thumb just for the trip. I can still smell those cedar shavings.

posts.quote: THE FEED STORE SOLD SEED BY THE SCOOP, AND THE SACKS WERE SEWN SHUT WITH A STRING YOU PULLED OPEN.
posts.caption: The feed store smelled like dust, grain, and burlap, and you could pick it out blindfolded from a block away. Wooden bins ran along the wall, each one with a brass scoop hanging on a nail. You told the clerk what you wanted, and he scooped it out onto a hanging scale and poured it into a paper sack. Then he sewed the top shut with a single line of chain stitch and left one loose end of string. One quick tug and the whole row unzipped, a trick every farm kid learned before he could tie his shoes. Nothing went to waste, not even the string, which ended up wrapped around a tomato plant.
posts.first: We kept a ball of that string in the kitchen drawer for years. It tied up beans, mended a kite, and once held a screen door shut through a whole winter.

posts.quote: MOM UNPLUGGED EVERYTHING DURING A THUNDERSTORM, AND WE WATCHED THE LIGHTNING FROM THE FRONT ROOM.
posts.caption: When the sky turned green and the first rumble rolled in, Mom went through the house like a general. The television came unplugged, then the toaster, then the radio, and she even pulled the cord on the lamp. We were not allowed on the telephone, and we were not allowed in the bathtub. So we sat in the front room in the half-dark with the curtains open and watched the storm do its work. Every flash lit up the whole street, and we counted the seconds until the thunder like it was a game. Nobody was scared, because she was right there on the arm of the couch.
posts.first: My mother also held a rosary through the loud ones and pretended she wasn't. When the power finally went out, my father lit a candle and told the same ghost story every time. We knew every word and begged for it anyway.

posts.quote: In November the whole town smelled like wet wool, woodsmoke, and somebody's pot roast.
posts.first: I can still tell you which house on our street had the pot roast going by the smell alone. It was always the one with the fogged-up kitchen window.

posts.quote: THE FLOOR VENT WAS THE WARMEST SPOT IN THE HOUSE, AND THE DOG ALWAYS GOT THERE FIRST.
posts.caption: On a cold morning the whole house had exactly one good spot, and it was a square iron grate in the hallway floor. Warm air came up from the furnace below with a faint smell of toasted dust. The dog found it before anyone else was out of bed, and he stretched across it like a rug. The kids stood in line at the edge, trading turns to hold their pajamas over the heat. Somebody always dropped a sock down it and spent the afternoon fishing it out with a coat hanger. It was the only place in the house nobody argued about sharing, mostly because the dog never moved.
posts.first: Our dog was a beagle named Duke, and he would not move for anybody except Dad. I stood on that grate in my socks every winter morning of my childhood. The pattern of it is still printed on my memory.

posts.quote: THE HALL PASS WAS A WOODEN BLOCK THE SIZE OF A BRICK, AND NOBODY WANTED TO BE THE ONE WHO LOST IT.
posts.caption: Our hall pass was a block of wood about as heavy as a brick, with a hole drilled through one end and a loop of rope through the hole. Mrs. Dunning kept it on a nail by the door, and nobody left the room without it. It was too big to hide in a pocket and too ugly to want to be seen with. You carried it down the hall with both hands like a loaf of bread and tried to look important. Every year one kid lost it on a bathroom trip, and the whole building searched until lunch. It always turned up behind a radiator, and the kid who lost it was famous until June.
posts.first: I lost it once, in the fourth grade. I can tell you it was in the boys' bathroom, behind the trash can, and I can tell you that I have never been so afraid of a piece of wood.
